# In Praise of Getting Lost

There is a particular quiet that arrives when a person realizes they are lost. The street you expected is not there. The shop on the corner has closed, moved, or apparently never existed. Your phone offers to help, but for a moment you resist it. For a few seconds, maybe a minute, the world is larger than your plans. You are standing in the wrong place, and the wrong place has a view.

I remember getting lost for the first time in a city I thought I knew. I was looking for a small public garden whose entrance I had seen on a map. I walked confidently for several blocks, then less confidently, and finally stopped beneath a tree while a bus passed with the unhurried indifference of public transport. I had forgotten the name of the street. More importantly, I had forgotten why I thought I knew the way. The garden was still there, somewhere, but my certainty had collapsed before I arrived. I found it eventually by asking someone. The journey took twenty minutes longer than it should have. I never forgot the embarrassment, but I also remember noticing things on the wrong street: a bakery with open doors, a cat asleep on a windowsill, a patch of sunlight falling across an old wall. Those things did not appear on the map. They would not have appeared in the version of the walk that went perfectly.

A map is one of civilization’s great acts of confidence. It takes a landscape full of infinite detail and compresses it into lines, symbols, colors, and distances. It declares that the territory can be held still long enough to be described. It promises that somewhere, in offices or institutions or the collective imagination, there is a correct version of where things are. Most of the time, the promise is useful. We need to know which bridge crosses the river, where the train station is, whether the road continues beyond the next bend. But a map is also an argument. It tells us which features matter, which connections deserve emphasis, and which spaces may safely be left blank. It is not a failure of a map to omit the smell of rain on pavement, but it is a failure if we forget that it has omitted them.

Childhood maps are often wonderfully inaccurate. Mine included a swimming pool that was at least three blocks from its actual location, a railway line that disappeared behind a hedge, and a mysterious path I had invented to avoid walking past a house where someone had once said something unkind. Distances were adjusted according to feeling rather than measurement. A destination that took twenty minutes to reach might be drawn close if I liked it; a place I disliked could be pushed toward the edge of the page. These maps were useless for navigation and excellent for memory. They recorded not only where I thought things were, but what I believed about them.

We tend to imagine that maps became more accurate before they became more personal. Certainly, modern maps have become more detailed, more searchable, and more responsive to our particular intentions. They can show the shortest route, the safest route, the route with a library, the route avoiding hills, the route that passes a particular kind of coffee shop. We can ask them to favor parks or avoid motorways. A contemporary map is less a picture of the territory than a set of suggestions about how to move through it. That is valuable. It is also a little unsettling. The map no longer simply tells us where we are. It tells us where we ought to go.

Before printed directions, getting lost was an ordinary part of moving through the world. People traveled by landmarks, stories, and the knowledge of locals. A guide might say that you could not miss a certain place, although it lay beyond two rivers and a stand of trees. A sign might point toward a village whose name most travelers had never heard. In unfamiliar places, people accepted a level of uncertainty that now feels excessive, even though their practical knowledge was often considerable. They knew how to read weather, seasons, animal behavior, the slope of the ground, and the changing color of the sky. They could be lost geographically without being helpless.

This does not mean that older travelers were automatically wise. Someone who was lost could still be exhausted, frightened, or late. Nor was every old map a masterpiece of mystery, filled with imaginative monsters and distant countries drawn from rumor. But older maps often admitted more about the limits of their knowledge. A blank region might remain blank. A coastline could fade into decorative uncertainty. The map did not always pretend that its information was equally trustworthy everywhere. In that respect, it occasionally offered a lesson we have since struggled to learn: not every space needs to be occupied by a label.

A wrong turn is one of the oldest forms of unplanned travel. It has produced some of the best stories precisely because nobody chose it. The person who accidentally enters a side street discovers a courtyard, a language lesson, an argument about a statue, or a view that becomes the reason they remember the entire trip. The famous discovery is usually presented as the work of a person who knew exactly what they were looking for, but many discoveries begin with a small failure of navigation. We call it a detour, as if the deviation were simply a technical matter of distance. Sometimes it is. Most of the time, a detour changes the route and the person taking it.

Not every wrong turn is a gift. Some are simply wrong. A missed train can mean a missed appointment, a missed exit can mean hours of delay, and a mistaken assumption about a neighborhood can have consequences that have nothing to the romance of wandering. The point is not that inconvenience is valuable in itself. The point is that the shortest path is not the only path capable of producing knowledge. Efficiency answers the question, “How do I get there?” It does not answer the questions that appear when the original route disappears.

The optimized world has little patience for this. Every journey is evaluated by duration, fuel consumption, energy expenditure, and the number of interruptions required. The fastest route is presented as the obvious one, even when the slower road passes a market, a reservoir, or a village with an excellent bakery. A navigation system can know that a street is pleasant before nine in the morning and congested afterward, but it cannot know that you have been sitting in an office for six hours and need to see a horizon. It can optimize for arrival while missing the journey entirely.

There is a deeper problem with this kind of optimization. When every route is judged by its usefulness, places that serve no immediate purpose become difficult to justify. A street with no destination at its end is suspicious. A park is good if it improves health, increases property value, or provides a pleasant view. A person who takes a walk without a destination may be assumed to be wasting time, though walking may be the activity that makes the rest of life possible. Efficiency is valuable. It becomes dangerous when it pretends to be the only form of value.

Getting lost also reveals how much our sense of direction depends on stories. We do not experience space as a blank grid. We experience it through memory and expectation. A shortcut is not merely a line between two points; it is the remembered path taken with someone, the route avoided because of a storm, the way home from a school where we once felt afraid. When those stories change, our physical surroundings can become strange. A familiar building is replaced. A shop becomes a bank. A tree that once marked the turning point is cut down. The city is still there, but the map inside the mind has failed to keep up.

This is one reason people sometimes become disoriented in places they have visited many times. The body remembers a route that no longer exists. The mind insists on a landmark that has vanished. We are not simply bad at directions; we are responding to an older arrangement of the world. A person who has relied on a particular street for years may feel genuinely lost when a construction fence blocks it, even if another route is perfectly available. Being lost can be a form of grief for a place that no longer exists.

The same is true of cities remembered through other people. A grandmother’s route to the bus stop may include a bakery that has since become an office block. A childhood shortcut may run through a field now covered by houses. The person who tells the story is not only giving directions. They are offering access to a version of the world that exists in memory. To be asked for help is therefore to be asked, “Can you show me how your world connects to mine?” The answer may come in the form of a detailed explanation, or it may be a simple gesture toward a steeple, a bridge, a particular tree, or a clock tower.

Strangers are unexpectedly good at this. They know the scale of the neighborhood in a way that a printed map cannot. They know which door sticks in wet weather, which crossing has no signal, where the pavement becomes muddy after rain, and which shortcut is only a shortcut for someone with long legs. Their instructions are full of practical wisdom. “Go past the place with the blue shutters.” “Take the next street after the church.” “You’ll see it when the road bends toward the hills.” These are not coordinates. They are relationships between things, and relationships are what memory is made of.

The person who asks for directions must also relinquish a little pride. A traveler with a carefully planned itinerary can usually find the answer alone, even if it takes longer. A lost person must admit that the local knowledge of a stranger is more useful than their own. That admission is often easier when the stakes are small. It becomes harder when the lostness is more serious: when someone has no safe place to return to, when a border has closed behind them, when the language on the signs is unfamiliar, when the map is not merely inaccurate but actively misleading.

We should therefore distinguish between the freedom to wander and the condition of being stranded. Most of us have the privilege of choosing unfamiliarity. We can take a wrong turn and expect to recover. We can miss a train and know that another will come. We can carry a charged phone, identification, money, and a sense of how to ask for help. Others do not have that luxury. For them, uncertainty is not a recreational state. It can mean danger, exploitation, deportation, violence, or simply the absence of any place where one is welcome. To praise getting lost is not to romanticize the experience of everyone who says they are lost. It is to notice that a map and a welcome are not the same thing.

There is also a danger in making novelty itself a goal. Some people travel only to collect experiences, and some experiences are exhausted quickly. A person can visit many places and remain remarkably uninterested in them. They may move from landmark to landmark, photograph each one, and return home with an album full of evidence that they have been elsewhere. The difficulty is not staying in one place. It is becoming unable to be present in any place. A new street is not necessarily an escape from routine if the person is carrying routine everywhere with them.

To get lost deliberately, then, is to become temporarily less goal-shaped. It is a practice of attention. Instead of asking only where the destination is, one can ask what is on the corner, why the street curves that way, which direction the wind is coming from, what the buildings are made of, and who might have chosen the names on them. These questions do not help a person arrive more quickly. They make arrival less important for a while.

The practice can begin on an ordinary walk. Leave the usual route at the next safe intersection. Walk without checking the phone for a few minutes. Choose a street because it looks interesting rather than because it is efficient. Sit on a bench with no purpose beyond sitting. Learn the name of a tree. Notice the difference between a street that is busy because people must pass through it and one that is busy because people have decided to stay. These are small acts, but they loosen the grip of habit. They restore the sense that the built environment is not a machine designed to move us from one predetermined point to another.

Maps are especially useful when they help us notice what we would otherwise overlook. A transit map can show the shape of a city’s history, which lines were built first, where the stations cluster, and how neighborhoods are connected or separated. A weather map can turn an apparently shapeless sky into patterns of pressure and wind. Even a map of a park can teach us to see a landscape as a set of designed relationships rather than an undifferentiated green space. The problem is not the map. It is the belief that the map is complete.

Every person carries a private cartography. It includes the grocery store where a friend first told them some difficult news, the corner where they once waited in the rain, the bench from which a child watched a procession, the shortcut that makes them feel briefly brave. Some of these locations are marked on public maps. None of them are marked in the ordinary sense. A favorite place is not primarily a coordinate. It is a relationship between a place and a version of oneself who has existed there.

This is why a city can be accurately mapped and still be unknown. A person may know all the street names and have no idea where to find a quiet place to think. They may know how to reach the center and not how to reach the river. They may possess perfect directions to a friend’s house and have no memory of the conversation that took place there. Official geography is not the whole geography of a life. The missing parts are often the parts that make us willing to return.

Getting lost with other people adds another dimension. Children are frequently better at it than adults because they have not yet learned to treat every detour as an error. A child may insist on inspecting a stick, a beetle, a puddle, or a patch of grass that everyone else would prefer to ignore. The group slows down. An adult becomes impatient. It means that their willingness to stop can interrupt the adult obsession with progress.

The modern world makes it increasingly difficult to be lost, and sometimes that is a good thing. Emergency services need accurate addresses. Airports need clear signs. Search-and-rescue teams need maps. There is no virtue in failing to read a warning sign or refusing directions when a person is exhausted, vulnerable, or far from home. We can respect efficiency without surrendering curiosity. We can recognize that the world contains much that cannot be reduced to our current purpose, and that not everything useful is visible from the center of our plan.

Getting lost is often described as a failure of navigation, but sometimes it is a success of imagination. It means allowing the mind to complete what the map leaves out. It permits the territory to exceed the description. It reminds us that a person can be competent, informed, and capable, and still not know everything. That combination is not a weakness to be eliminated. It is one of the conditions of being alive.

The return journey matters too. A person who has been lost may arrive at the correct place with a different sense of it. The fountain is where the map said it would be, but the person seeing it has changed. The route has included hunger, confusion, an unexpected conversation, and a few minutes in which no instruction was guiding them. The destination does not erase those minutes. It becomes part of their meaning.

Maybe this is why the wrong turn is so often worth retelling. The story is not really about the destination. It is about the moment when certainty fell away and the world reopened. We remember the embarrassment because it makes the event legible, but we also remember the light on the old wall, the stranger who pointed the way, the street that seemed impossible on paper and yet led somewhere real. The story has a lesson, though the lesson is not always “be careful.” Sometimes the lesson is simply: you did not know what was beyond the turn.

A life can have destinations without being only a sequence of arrivals. It can contain streets that were never on the plan, conversations with people we did not expect to meet, and days whose value cannot be calculated from their usefulness. To get lost is to discover that possibility, if only briefly. It is to step outside the route and discover that the world has not been waiting obediently to be crossed.

The map can go back into the drawer. The phone can be put away. And for a while, the destination can wait.
